newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NEW EU LAW TO HELP LAWYERS PRACTICE ABROAD.
newsitem.headline: NEW EU LAW TO HELP LAWYERS PRACTICE ABROAD.

text.p: European Union internal market ministers agreed rules on Wednesday to make it easier for lawyers to set up a permanent practice elsewhere in the 15-nation bloc.
But Luxembourg said it opposed the proposed legislation and might challenge it in the EU court, an EU official said.
The EU directive, which also needs the approval of the European Parliament, aims to make it easier for lawyers to establish a practice in an EU country other than the one where they qualified.

Under the directive, lawyers can either practice under their home-country professional title for an unlimited period or seek admission to the profession of lawyer in the member state where they are working after three years.

A lawyer working under a home-country professional title would be able to carry out the same activities as a colleague from that member state, giving advice on the law of the home member state, on EU and international law and the law of the host country.
Lawyers who just want to provide services in another member state may already do so under an EU law agreed 20 years ago.
As part of the drive to establish a single market, the EU also adopted legislation in 1988 on the mutual recognition of higher-education diplomas.
But it gave member states the right to insist on applicants passing a test on their knowledge of the country's law, in effect an obstacle to the freedom of establishment.
Apart from those in Luxembourg, lawyers were expected to welcome Wednesday's decision. Luxembourg which, as a European
banking centre, is home for many foreign EU lawyers, particularly opposed the idea that lawyers could practice for an unlimited period without obtaining the professional title of the host country.
It also said that the directive should be adopted under EU treaty rules requiring unanimity, and not by a majority decision.
